title: Wynn's Midnight Frolics band
summary: Wynn took a jazz band into the Midnight Frolics in the fading district.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Was that still the district up there?

That was the district. That was the last. That was the last. The district was fading, but there still was a slight resemblance of it. I mean Bloom, the name of Artie Bloom I think still had the Frolics there. And well of course they had terrific shows and they had big shows. Ralph Edwards had the house band there. So they wanted a band just to play at animation time. So what happened, this, before then they had a lot of flow entertainers, you know, with the small pianos and the girl singers. They would push them all around and doing the animation they would sing. So he got the idea that he wanted some real jazz music in there instead of entertainers. So I had my to get connection for the thing. This same fellow who was a very good friend of mine from the All of Us drummer, Francois Mosley, his brother was a caretaker and pulled her there for the place. So when the man come up with the idea, he shoots it right on to me. So I go down and talk with the fellow. Well he was set on Earl. Who he really wanted was Earl Heinze. So he said, well I will give you this job if you can get the Earl Heinze. So I said, well I doubted very much. I said, I think it's almost impossible. I think it's just about impossible to get Earl. But I said, there's another real great jazz artist that I can get. Song sure I could get him. Why I knew I could get Lurie, because Lurie was working at the Vendome Theater, see. He was in the pit with Erskine Tate at that time. And they were through about a quarter to eleven or something like that. Well now and then we didn't start until eleven or eleven fifteen or something like that. So that would be a double for him, see. So I talked this fellow into him, I said well just hear the outfit if you don't like it. There's nothing lost but a little time. So he said okay. So I got Lurie and this boy that had been in Lurie's band, George Terence and little Joe Walker. I got Peck on guitar and this boy, the drummer. The drummer from the All-Irland Service. I was just talking about his brother worked in the play. Mosley. Mosley, Francois Mosley and myself. And we went down there, Lurie was really blowing there. So we went down there and made the audacious man and said yeah this is it, this is great, this is great. So we start to work there. We start to work there and everybody's real happy. It's a terrific spot. I mean the place is packed in the jam all the time. It's a lively crowd and everything. So we do about two weeks there. And one night in the middle of the night everybody struck in the place. Say if you keep, if you keep that band there we all would walk out. All the electric, the electricians and the waiters and everything. I mean it was just one of those things. Because during that time there was a friction between, they say you trying to bring 35th street to 22nd street. There was a friction between number 10 and 208. And of course he had laid off, that was in the Spoden district, and he had laid off a lot of these girls, singers who was Dublin and a lot of the regular fellas around there had laid off. So they were all hot about those things. So in the middle of the night, I mean everybody said well this is it. The whole thing stopped. The place is packed in jam. And all people used to come out of here. And then Sophie Tuck and all of them, they were in town. They would be there every night. And the food was blowing. There wasn't any question. It was a man saying well what can I do. You see what's happening. You see what's happening. So he was nice enough. He said I'll give you boys two weeks out. He paid us for two weeks. He was the most hype person because he liked, I mean when we went in there it was in the winter time and he'd show us where our showers and everything was for the summer. You know. And everybody said well look like we set. You know. And this incident had to happen. So he was nice enough which he didn't have to do. He paid us for two weeks in advance. And called the whole thing off. So that was that. Well when you worked with Jimmy Noon, if you could tell a little bit about that. Yeah well I worked with Jimmy Noon. I did some work with him. But when I first come back from Europe I worked with Jimmy in I guess it would be early 33. He got a band together, a new spot open, a very beautiful place on 55th Street, Club Morocco. So I went in there with him. I worked a while with him in there. In fact we worked until the place folded. Yeah. It was a new venture. You ever recorded with Jimmy Noon? I never did.
